title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.5.1-c06, 4.5.1-c05, 4.5.1-c07, 4.5.1-c02. Clues: 4.5.1-c06 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c05 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c07 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c02 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.1-q01, 4.5.1-q02, 4.5.1-q03, 4.5.1-q04, 4.5.1-q05, 4.5.1-q06, 4.5.1-q07, 4.5.1-q08, 4.5.1-q09, 4.5.1-q10, 4.5.1-q11, 4.5.1-q12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Oxidation
items.clue: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.

items.label: Combustion
items.clue: The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy.

items.label: Neutralisation
items.clue: The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water.

items.label: Surroundings
items.clue: Everything outside the reacting chemicals themselves, including the solvent, the container and the air.

questions.stem: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What must be true of the product molecules?

options.text: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount given out.
They have less energy, and the energy released no longer exists.
They have exactly the same total energy as the reactants did.

questions.explanation: This is the specification's own statement: the energy that reached the surroundings came from the chemicals, so the products sit lower by exactly that amount.

questions.stem: Which statement about energy during a chemical reaction is correct?

options.text: No energy is transferred to or from the surroundings at all.
The total energy in the universe is the same after the reaction as before.
Some of the energy is destroyed as the surroundings are being warmed.
Reactants and products always contain exactly equal energy.

questions.explanation: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions; the reaction only moves energy between the chemicals and their surroundings.

questions.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It transfers energy out, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It stores the energy inside the products, so nothing warms up.

questions.explanation: This is the specification definition: energy goes out to the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings increases.

questions.stem: Which of these reactions is exothermic?

options.text: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
the reaction inside a sports injury cold pack
citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate
the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali

questions.explanation: Neutralisation is one of the three exothermic examples named by the specification, alongside combustion and many oxidation reactions.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon is lit with a Bunsen flame and burns brightly, warming the tripod above it. Why is this reaction described as exothermic?

options.text: Energy had to be supplied by the flame, so energy is taken in overall here.
Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, and that is why the tripod warms.
The oxidation takes in energy from the surrounding air, making it glow.
Burning stores the energy in the magnesium oxide that is produced.

questions.explanation: Combustion is exothermic; the flame only starts it, and the energy warming the tripod comes out of the chemicals.

questions.stem: A hand warmer contains iron powder that oxidises slowly once the pack is opened. Why does the pack become warm?

options.text: The pack takes energy in from your own hand, and this is what makes it warm.
The reaction is endothermic, so it lets out the heat it had stored.
The oxidation is exothermic and transfers energy to your hands and the air.
Slow reactions give out no energy; the padding keeps hands warm.

questions.explanation: Many oxidation reactions are exothermic, and the specification names hand warmers as an everyday use of one.

questions.stem: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature will rise.
It gives out energy, and so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It releases the energy that was stored inside the reactants.
It takes energy in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.

questions.explanation: This is the specification definition: energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

questions.stem: Copper carbonate is heated strongly and breaks down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. Why is this reaction endothermic?

options.text: Energy is taken in to break the compound down.
Energy is given out because a hot flame is used here.
Energy is stored, then released as the gas escapes.
Energy is destroyed as the carbonate breaks apart.

questions.explanation: Thermal decompositions are endothermic: energy has to be supplied continuously from the surroundings for the compound to break down.

questions.stem: Citric acid solution is stirred with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the thermometer falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, as the fizzing shows energy leaving.
The reaction is exothermic, since the chemicals have lost energy.
The reaction is endothermic and takes energy in from the surroundings.
No energy was transferred, as 6 °C is too small a change.

questions.explanation: The temperature of the surroundings has decreased, which is the specification's test for an endothermic reaction; this pair is its named example.

questions.stem: A student measures the temperature of the surroundings before and after four reactions. Which result shows an endothermic reaction?

options.text: The temperature rose from 22.0 °C to 31.5 °C during this reaction.
The temperature rose from 16.5 °C to 22.0 °C as it went along.
The temperature stayed at 22.0 °C throughout the reaction.
The temperature fell from 22.0 °C to 16.5 °C during the reaction.

questions.explanation: A fall in the temperature of the surroundings is exactly how the specification says an endothermic reaction is recognised.

questions.stem: During a neutralisation the thermometer in the mixture rises by 8 °C. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: It has been transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings.
It has been transferred from the surroundings and into the chemicals.
The chemicals still hold the very same energy they had before.
It has been stored in the salt and the water that are made.

questions.explanation: The solution is part of the surroundings, so a rise in its temperature shows energy leaving the chemicals: an exothermic reaction.

questions.stem: A sports injury pack and a hand warmer each rely on a chemical reaction. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: The injury pack is exothermic; the hand warmer is endothermic.
The injury pack is endothermic and the warmer exothermic.
Both are exothermic, but the injury pack releases energy slowly.
Both are endothermic, and each takes energy from the skin.

questions.explanation: The pack must take energy in from the surroundings to cool a swelling, while the warmer must transfer energy out to the hands.
